title.en: Language work for Spectacular Wonders: synonyms, binomials, participles, gerunds and a descriptive essay

text.en: The chapter Spectacular Wonders describes living root bridges, a rare crater lake, glowing seas and a rainbow mountain. Its language work teaches us to say such wonders in richer words, to use fixed word pairs, and to use verbs as adjectives and as nouns.

keepEnglishTerms: came into existence, in full glory
came into existence, to name a few, in full glory, in disbelief, to no end, age-old problem

text.en:
Some expressions in the chapter come as a ready-made group, such as came into existence, to name a few, in full glory, in disbelief, to no end and age-old problem. We learn them as whole expressions and use them in our own sentences.
Came into existence means began to exist, as in 'The town came into existence around a river crossing'. In full glory means at its most beautiful, as in 'The orchard stood in full glory in spring'.
To no end means a great deal or without stopping, in disbelief means not able to believe, and to name a few means that only some examples are given from many. An age-old problem is a trouble that has lasted for a very long time.
A synonym is a word with nearly the same meaning as another word. The chapter gives us five strong adjectives: enigmatic means mysterious and puzzling, colossal means huge and gigantic, spectacular means stunning and awe-inspiring, serene means calm and peaceful, and exotic means unusual and foreign.
Choosing a stronger synonym makes writing vivid. Instead of 'a big mountain' you can write 'a colossal mountain', and instead of 'a quiet lake' you can write 'a serene lake'. A thesaurus is a book or website that lists synonyms.
A binomial is a pair of fixed words joined by 'and' or 'or', in a set order. The chapter uses hide-and-seek and flora and fauna. The pairs may be synonyms, opposites, rhyming words or words that start with the same sound.
Learn these binomials with their meanings. Odds and ends means small unimportant things. On and off means sometimes. Mix and match means put different things together to get many combinations. All or nothing means something done completely or not at all.
Part and parcel means a necessary part of something. Pick and choose means choose only the best. Sooner or later means at some time in the future. Leaps and bounds means increasing or developing very fast. We cannot swap the order of a binomial, so we say 'odds and ends', never 'ends and odds'.
A participle is a verb form that works like an adjective. The living root bridges, a striking contrast and rugged terrain use living, striking and rugged to describe nouns.
A present participle usually ends in -ing and describes an action that is going on, such as a glowing sea or a moving light. A past participle usually ends in -ed, -d, -t, -en or -n and describes an action that is finished, such as carved stone or scattered islands. Irregular verbs may differ.
A gerund is also an -ing verb form, but it works as a noun. In 'Crossing the waterways was difficult', crossing is a gerund because it is the subject. So the test is simple: if the -ing word describes a noun, it is a participle, and if it names an activity and acts like a noun, it is a gerund.
A gerund can be the subject, as in 'Swimming is fun'. It can be a subject complement, as in 'Her passion is painting'. It can be the object of a verb, as in 'I enjoy reading', and the object of a preposition, as in 'She is interested in learning'. It also follows certain verbs, such as avoid talking.
We can join two short sentences with a participle or a gerund. 'Nitesh entered the room. He saw his friend' becomes 'Entering the room, Nitesh saw his friend'. The participle phrase tells us what happened first, and both sentences must share the same doer.
For the listening task, listen to the talk on the rainbow mountain with a purpose. Before listening, read the six statements, and while listening, tick only those that match what the speakers actually say. Do not tick a statement just because it sounds likely.
For the speaking task, work in a group of four and present a place of interest in your region over about ten slides. Cover the choice of place, where it is and how to reach it, its attractions and history, weather and food, and the best time to visit.
For the writing task, write a descriptive essay about something in nature that caught your attention, with a title. Use an introduction of one paragraph, a body of two or three paragraphs and a conclusion of one paragraph, and use vivid words such as serene, colossal and spectacular.

problem.en: Underline the participle or gerund in each sentence and say which it is. (a) The glowing waves lit up the shore. (b) Climbing the cliff takes courage.

text.en: (a) 'Glowing' describes the noun 'waves', so it is a present participle.

why.en: A participle works as an adjective.

text.en: (b) 'Climbing the cliff' is the subject of the sentence, so 'climbing' is a gerund.

why.en: A gerund works as a noun.

text.en: Check each time by asking: does the word describe a noun, or does it name an activity? That decides participle or gerund.

prompt.en: Explain the difference between a participle and a gerund with one example of each, and say what a binomial is.

Changing the order of words in a binomial

points.en: Expressions such as in full glory and to name a few are learnt as whole groups.
Synonyms: enigmatic = mysterious, colossal = huge, spectacular = stunning, serene = calm, exotic = unusual.
A binomial is a fixed pair joined by and or or, such as part and parcel.
A participle works as an adjective; a gerund is an -ing word that works as a noun.
A descriptive essay has a title, one introduction paragraph, two or three body paragraphs and a conclusion.
